# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code

**seeding**
: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

**base build**
: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.

**old code**
: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.

Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.

## Finding or building a base build

- If your brief names a base build, use it.
- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.

      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
      ant compileAll
      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean

If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.

## Seeding a worktree

A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.

Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.

    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]

- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.

## Running the old code

If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.

`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:

    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM

- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).

To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:

    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss

The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".

A trait declaration contains a set of method declarations.
Syntactically, a method declaration begins with
an optional sequence of modifiers followed by
the method's name,
optional static parameters
(described in \chapref{trait-parameters}),
the value parameter with its (optionally) declared type,
an optional type of a return value,
an optional declaration of thrown checked exceptions
(discussed in \chapref{exceptions}),
an optional \KWD{where} clause
(discussed in \secref{where-clauses}),
a contract for the method (discussed in \secref{method-contracts}),
and finally an optional body expression preceded by the token \EXP{=}.
If a method declaration has the \KWD{getter} modifier,
it does not affect the behavior of a program; rather,
it documents that the method is intended to serve as a getter.
A \KWD{throws} clause does not include naked type variables.
Every element in a \KWD{throws} clause is a subtype of
\TYP{CheckedException}.


Method declarations can include the following special modifiers:
\paragraph{\KWD{getter}:}
A method declaration with the modifier \KWD{getter} explicitly declares a
getter method for a field, even in the absence of an actual field declaration.
\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
If such a field exists, there is no implicit getter for the field.
An explicitly declared getter method must take no arguments and return a
result of the field's type.
A getter method must not throw any checked exception.
Getter names may not overlap ordinary method names.
A getter method must be invoked with the field access syntax:
%expr.id
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{expr}.\VAR{id}\)
\end{Fortress}
where \VAR{id} is the name of the getter method.



\paragraph{\KWD{setter}:}
A method declaration with the modifier \KWD{setter} explicitly declares a
setter method for a field, even in the absence of an actual field.
\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
If such a field exists, there is no implicit setter for the field.
An explicitly declared setter method must take a single argument---the
value being set---and return \EXP{()}.
A setter method must not throw any checked exception.
Setter names may not overlap ordinary method names.
A setter method must be invoked with the \emph{assignment syntax}:
%expr1.id := expr2
\begin{Fortress}
\({expr}_{1}.\VAR{id} \ASSIGN {expr}_{2}\)
\end{Fortress}


We say that a method declaration \emph{occurs} in a trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{declares} a method declaration that occurs
in that trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{inherits} method declarations from the
declarations of its immediate supertraits
except those method declarations
that are \emph{overridden} (as described later in this section) or
whose parameter type (not including the type of the self parameter)
is equal to the parameter type of a method declaration
that occurs in the trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{provides} the method declarations that it
declares or inherits.




There are two sorts of method declarations:
\emph{dotted method} declarations and
\emph{functional method} declarations.
Syntactically, a dotted method declaration is identical to a function
declaration.
When a method is invoked, a special self parameter is bound to the
object on which it is invoked.



A functional method declaration has a parameter named \KWD{self} at an
arbitrary position in its parameter list.  This parameter is not given a type
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.
\revision{revival-self-type}{In a trait \VAR{T} with a self-type parameter \VAR{X}
(\secref{trait-decls}), this remains the type of the \KWD{self} parameter
in the declaration's signature, which overloading and the choice of a declaration
at a call read, save the test of whether two overloaded declarations' parameter
types exclude each other, which reads it as \EXP{T \cap X}; in the method's body
\KWD{self} has the type \EXP{T \cap X} (\secref{idn-ref}).}
Semantically, functional method declarations can be viewed as top-level
function declarations.  For example, the following overloaded functional method

\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.a.tex}

Functional method declarations may be overloaded with top-level function
declarations.
An abstract function declaration
(described in \secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations})
can be provided also for overloaded functional method declarations.
See \chapref{multiple-dispatch} for a discussion of overloaded
functionals in Fortress.

When a method declaration includes a body expression, it is called a
\emph{method definition}.
A method declaration that does not have its body expression is referred to
as an \emph{abstract method declaration}.
An abstract method declaration declares an \emph{abstract method};
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method: a method definition with the same name and the self parameter (if any)
at the same position whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self
parameter, is that of the abstract method declaration, or definitions whose
parameter types are subtypes of it and together cover it
(\secref{internal-types}), or it is a static error.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said only that
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method.
The object defines the method by a body at its parameter type, or by bodies at
narrower parameter types that together cover it, \KWD{comprises} clauses read
at the level of values (\secref{trait-decls}), as
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} asks of the concrete declarations for an
abstract function declaration; one body at a narrower parameter type that does
not cover the abstract method's does not define it.
This is the rule of the type group's compiled type checker (2012) and of its
calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012).
The requirement of \secref{object-decls} that an object define all abstract
methods inherited from its supertraits is unchanged: it defines them in this
sense.}
An abstract method declaration may include the modifier \KWD{abstract}.
It may elide parameter names but parameter
types cannot be omitted except for the self parameter.


\note{
Method declarations that are overridden by some declaration are not
accessible.  They are not considered for overloading checks.

Partial overriding of an overloaded functional is allowed
but partial overriding of a functional declaration is not allowed.
}

A method declaration may have the modifier \KWD{override}.
Such a declaration \emph{overrides} any inherited declaration with the same name
and the self parameter (if any) at the same position,
whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self parameter,
is a strict subtype of the overriding declaration's parameter type.
The return type of the overriding declaration must be subtype of
that of the overridden declaration to preserve type safety.
A declaration with the modifier \KWD{override} must override
some inherited declaration.
It is a static error if a declaration with the modifier \KWD{override}
does not override any inherited declaration.

# Climb batch 35: the judge's ruling on the merged-diff review

Decision: **repair**, of specification text and records only. One clause of an Appendix I effect is narrowed, and the FACTS entry and the gather's record line that restate it follow. No source, library, checker, interpreter or test file changes, so the gate does not run again: a repair reruns the gate only where it changes a path under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or `build.xml`, outside the test files, and `Specification/` and `explorations/` are not among those paths (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:1336-1337`, `gateReads`, applied by `repairRerun` at `:1452-1457`; the skill's `gate.md`, "When to run it"). The edit adds no example, so `ant testSpecData` (P-124) reads nothing it changes. It is not **land**: the settlement edits `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, and the land rule admits only tests and records.

The review's routed finding (review-routed.1, the test owed where rungs S and O meet, `PLAN.md:943`) goes to the next batch as the review routed it; I give it no ruling. The review's own record fixes (`b0a5943e76`, `explorations/` only) are not contested and stand. I did not read the gate's output.

## The finding, upheld

`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:6423-6425`, in the effect of the entry "The features not yet supported, in the preface and the introduction" (`\seclabel{revival-supported}`, `:6367`), reads: "the compiled type checker refuses an \KWD{override} in a generic trait over a declaration that the trait inherits under a \KWD{where} clause (row~1107)." The gather wrote it in O's commit `d56eb8a882` (its message: "the gather's correction"; `climb-batch-35/RECORD.md:131`).

The code refuses less than that:

- `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:384-385` extends the type analyzer with the trait's static parameters and `None`: a `where` clause of an `extends` entry is not held, so the clause's static parameter keeps its declared bound. Row 1107's note says the same: "The overloading check reads `A`'s `f` with `T` unbounded, the condition not held".
- `:410-411` reads what the trait provides, and which own declaration overrides which inherited one, on that analyzer (`STypesUtil.providedAndOverridden`). `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1715-1716` pairs an `override` with an inherited declaration whose parameter types are equivalent to, or below, its own.
- `OverloadingChecker.scala:424` (`checkOverridesSomething`, `:755-789`) refuses an `override` that is in no pair.

So an inherited declaration whose parameter types do not name the clause's static parameter is read exactly, and an `override` over it is accepted. The reviewer's probe shows it on the merged code (`e922c2ea1a`): with `override g(x: Number)` in `G` over `A`'s `g(x: ZZ32)`, `bin/fortress typecheck` and `bin/fortress compile` exit 0 and `bin/fortress run` prints `G`; with `override f(x: ZZ32)` over `A`'s `f(x: T)` added, the checker refuses: 'Invalid override of f in trait G: (G[\T\], ZZ32)->String ... has the modifier override and does not override any inherited declaration.', 'Invalid overloading of f in trait G'. The sentence names every override over a declaration inherited under a `where` clause, so it is false of the first program.

The rule broken: an effect names each departure with its ledger row, so that "the text claims no more than holds" (the skill's `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree"; P-95, "Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason."). Row 1107's own claim names only the inherited declaration whose parameter type is the clause's static parameter.

## Which claims were right

- The reviewer: right that the clause is broader than the code and than row 1107's claim, and right that the repair needs no gate.
- The reviewer's suggested wording, "... and whose parameter type is that clause's static parameter (row~1107)", may still claim more than the code at one point. By `STypesUtil.scala:1716`, an `override` whose parameter type lies above the static parameter's declared bound, as `override f(x: Any)` over `f(x: T)` with `T` bounded by `Any`, is paired as an override even with the clause not held, so the checker would accept it. I ran nothing (my role runs no program); step 1 below settles it with one typecheck, and step 2 picks the wording by its result.
- The gather: wrong in `climb-batch-35/RECORD.md:131`, "each clause checked against `CodeGen.checkOverrideCompilable` ... and `OverloadingChecker.scala:410-411`, `:424`. Each states what the code does": the row-1107 clause did not. The same over-reach is in F-400 ("the checker refuses an override under a conditional extension that walk runs (row 1107)"), which the review did not name; it follows the repair, since FACTS binds later work.
- Rung O: its own records are exact. `rung-override-compiled/REPORT.md:84`, `:88` and `:134` and row 1107 name the one form tested.

## The repair

1. On the merged tree, with a private caches folder as the reviewer used, write and type check this program (`bin/fortress typecheck`, not `compile`: the code generator refuses an override over a declaration that names a static parameter, row 1106):

       component OverrideAboveBoundProbe
       export Executable
       trait A[\T\]
         f(x: T): String = "A"
       end
       trait G[\T\] extends A[\T\] where { T extends ZZ32 }
         override f(x: Any): String = "G"
       end
       object O extends G[\ZZ32\] end
       run(): () = println(O.f(3))
       end

- F-400 **The code generator compiles the modifier `override` by the checker's table of what an override keeps from being inherited, and the checker refuses an `override` that overrides nothing.** A trait's or an object's class holds the override and, at each hidden declaration's JVM signature, a bridge that runs it; no method runs the hidden declaration, and a dispatch over the override and the declarations of its name that it does not override is still written (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1798-1812`, `overriddenNotProvided`; `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1224-1237`, `overrideBridges`; `:1476-1484`, `dumpOverloadedMethodChaining`). The checker refuses an `override` that appears in no overriding pair of `providedAndOverridden`, equal parameter types included, as the traits chapter and walk do: 'Invalid override of f in object B: ... has the modifier override and does not override any inherited declaration.' (`scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:424`, `:763-789`). Two forms stay code-generator walls, an override of or by a method with static parameters of its own, and one in a generic type whose parameter types name a static parameter (row 1106); the checker refuses an override under a conditional extension that walk runs (row 1107) and checks none in an object expression (row 1108); under walk an object's override hides every inherited declaration of its name (row 1109). So a program may write `override` on the compiled path wherever no static parameter is involved. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

# Climb batch 33b: the repair after the merged-diff review

Written on `main` above `b3bfdf2526`, the judge's ruling (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-33b/JUDGE-review.md`). One launch of the repair worked this stage: no earlier `REPAIR-review.md` was in the batch folder, and `git status` of the main tree was clean at the start. Only `Specification/`, rung G's `REPORT.md`, this folder's `RECORD.md` and this file are edited. Nothing was built but the specification, and no test was added or run: an edit of the specification has no test (`SKILL.md`, "Rules for every task").

Then `git clean -fXq -- Specification`; `Specification/fortress.pdf` not updated. |
| 5 | `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-varargs/REPORT.md`, "Sentences of the specification made false": two items after the `preamble.tex:84` item, each with its text at `c799851472`, marked as found by the merged-diff review and changed by this repair, with its new text. |
| 6 | `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-33b/RECORD.md`, rung G's section: one line after the gather's notes, with the finding, the judge's addition, the two passages and the build's lines. |

The Effect of Appendix I's revival-supported entry, as the gather wrote it in rung O's commit d56eb8a882, said that the compiled type checker refuses an override in a generic trait over any declaration that the trait inherits under a where clause. The Effect now says that the checker reads the inherited declaration without the clause's bound and refuses an override that overrides it only by that bound; F-400's clause and row 1107's claim say the same, and the gather's RECORD.md names the narrowing. The specification built with no warning. REPAIR-review.md records the steps and three deviations of form from the judge's ruling. No source, library or test file changes.
